claim: Death domains (DDs) mediate assembly of oligomeric complexes for activation of downstream signaling pathways through incompletely understood mechanisms.
source: Death domains (DDs) mediate assembly of oligomeric complexes for activation of downstream signaling pathways through incompletely understood mechanisms.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field, drawing from established scientific understanding.

claim: The DD of p75 neurotrophin receptor (p75NTR) forms complexes with RhoGDI for activation of the RhoA pathway.
source: Here we report structures of complexes formed by the DD of p75 neurotrophin receptor (p75NTR) with RhoGDI, for activation of the RhoA pathway
evidence: The manuscript reports NMR structures and biochemical characterization of the DD:RhoGDI complex.

claim: The DD of p75NTR forms complexes with caspase recruitment domain (CARD) of RIP2 kinase for activation of the NF-kB pathway.
source: with caspase recruitment domain (CARD) of RIP2 kinase, for activation of the NF-kB pathway
evidence: The manuscript reports NMR structures and biochemical characterization of the DD:CARD complex.

claim: The p75NTR DD forms dimers with itself.
source: and with itself, revealing how DD dimerization controls access of intracellular effectors to the receptor.
evidence: The manuscript reports NMR structure of the DD homodimer.

claim: RIP2 CARD and RhoGDI bind to p75NTR DD at partially overlapping epitopes.
source: RIP2 CARD and RhoGDI bind to p75NTR DD at partially overlapping epitopes
evidence: The manuscript presents structural data showing overlapping binding sites on the p75NTR DD.

claim: RIP2 CARD binds to p75NTR DD with over 100-fold higher affinity than RhoGDI.
source: with over 100-fold difference in affinity
evidence: The manuscript presents SPR data showing Kd values of 4.67 nM for CARD and 0.82 μM for RhoGDI.

claim: RIP2 recruitment displaces RhoGDI from p75NTR upon ligand binding.
source: revealing the mechanism by which RIP2 recruitment displaces RhoGDI upon ligand binding.
evidence: The manuscript presents NMR competition studies and functional data supporting this mechanism.

claim: The p75NTR DD forms non-covalent, low-affinity symmetric dimers in solution.
source: The p75NTR DD forms non-covalent, low-affinity symmetric dimers in solution.
evidence: The manuscript presents NMR structure and biophysical characterization of the DD dimer.

claim: The p75NTR DD dimer interface overlaps with RIP2 CARD binding site.
source: The dimer interface overlaps with RIP2 CARD but not RhoGDI binding sites
evidence: The manuscript presents structural comparison showing overlap between dimer interface and CARD binding site.

claim: The p75NTR DD dimer interface does not overlap with RhoGDI binding site.
source: The dimer interface overlaps with RIP2 CARD but not RhoGDI binding sites
evidence: The manuscript presents structural comparison showing no overlap between dimer interface and RhoGDI binding site.

claim: Receptor activation is triggered by separation of DDs.
source: supporting a model of receptor activation triggered by separation of DDs.
evidence: The manuscript presents structural and functional data supporting this model, including FRET anisotropy measurements.

claim: The death domain (DD) is a globular protein module of 80–90 amino acid residues with a characteristic six-helix bundle fold.
source: The death domain (DD) is a globular protein module of 80–90 amino acid residues with a characteristic six-helix bundle fold (Feinstein et al., 1995; Ferrao and Wu, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: DDs are present in several members of the tumor necrosis factor receptor superfamily (TNFRSF).
source: DDs are present in a variety of proteins, including several members of the tumor necrosis factor receptor superfamily (TNFRSF) and a range of intracellular signaling components, such as caspases and kinases.
evidence: This is established knowledge about DD-containing proteins.

claim: The DD family includes four subfamilies: canonical DD, death effector domain (DED), caspase recruitment domain (CARD), and pyrin domain (PYD).
source: The DD family includes four subfamilies of structurally related domains, including the canonical DD, the death effector domain (DED), the caspase recruitment domain (CARD), and the pyrin domain (PYD).
evidence: This is established knowledge about DD superfamily classification.

claim: DD-containing proteins play central roles in apoptotic and inflammatory signaling through the formation of oligomeric protein complexes.
source: DD-containing proteins play central roles in apoptotic and inflammatory signaling through the formation of oligomeric protein complexes, and several disease-causing mutations have been mapped to DD interfaces (Park et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: All DD complexes described so far involve homotypic interactions between DDs of the same subfamily.
source: All DD complexes described so far involve homotypic interactions between DDs of the same subfamily (e.g., DD with DD, CARD with CARD, etc.).
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field prior to this study.

claim: All known DD interactions belong to one of three types (I to III), each mediated by conserved asymmetric interfaces.
source: All known DD interactions belong to one of three types (I to III), each mediated by conserved asymmetric interfaces in the interacting DDs (Park, 2011; Park et al., 2007; Weber and Vincenz, 2001).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Heterotypic complexes between DDs from different subfamilies have not yet been described prior to this study.
source: Heterotypic complexes between DDs from different subfamilies have not yet been described
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field prior to this study.

claim: The cytoplasmic domain of p75NTR contains a C-terminal DD connected to the transmembrane domain by a 60-residue-long linker region.
source: The cytoplasmic domain of the p75 neurotrophin receptor (p75NTR, also known as NGFR and TNFRSF16) contains a C-terminal DD connected to the transmembrane (TM) domain by a 60-residue-long linker region (Liepinsh, 1997).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: p75NTR is a receptor for members of the neurotrophin family, such as nerve growth factor (NGF) and brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF).
source: p75NTR is a receptor for members of the neurotrophin family, such as nerve growth factor (NGF) and brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) (Dechant and Barde, 2002; Roux and Barker, 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Beta-amyloid peptide can engage or signal through p75NTR.
source: In addition to the neurotrophins, a number of other extracellular ligands can also engage or signal through p75NTR, including the beta-amyloid peptide (Knowles et al., 2009; Perini et al., 2002)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The rabies virus glycoprotein can engage or signal through p75NTR.
source: the rabies virus glycoprotein (Tuffereau et al., 1998)
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Various myelin-derived polypeptides can engage or signal through p75NTR.
source: and various myelin-derived polypeptides (Wang et al., 2002; Wong et al., 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: p75NTR may function alone or in conjunction with other transmembrane proteins to allow ligand binding and intracellular signaling.
source: p75NTR may function alone or in conjunction with other transmembrane proteins to allow ligand binding and intracellular signaling.
evidence: This is established knowledge about p75NTR function.

claim: Members of the Trk family of receptor tyrosine kinases can function with p75NTR.
source: These proteins include members of the Trk family of receptor tyrosine kinases, members of the Vps10p family of sorting receptors, such as Sortilin, and the Nogo receptor, which promotes binding to myelin-derived ligands (Underwood and Coulson, 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The RhoA pathway regulated by p75NTR regulates axon growth, collapse and degeneration.
source: p75NTR can engage different intracellular pathways, of which the best characterized are the RhoA pathway, which regulates axon growth, collapse and degeneration (Park et al., 2010; Yamashita et al., 1999; Yamashita and Tohyama, 2003)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The NF-kB pathway regulated by p75NTR contributes to cell survival.
source: the NF-kB pathway, which contributes to cell survival (Carter et al., 1996; Khursigara et al., 2001; Vicario et al., 2015)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The c-Jun kinase (JNK) or caspase pathway regulated by p75NTR mediates apoptotic cell death.
source: and the c-Jun kinase (JNK) or caspase pathway, which mediates apoptotic cell death (Friedman, 2000; Yoon et al., 1998).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: p75NTR signaling through the RhoA, NF-kB, and JNK/caspase pathways requires a functional DD.
source: p75NTR signaling through any of those three pathways requires a functional DD (Charalampopoulos et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to previous literature from the authors' laboratory.

claim: Expression of p75NTR increases in a number of neurodegenerative diseases and upon injury or stress conditions.
source: Expression of p75NTR increases in a number of neurodegenerative diseases and upon injury or stress conditions, where it contributes to neuronal and glial cell damage, axonal degeneration, and synaptic dysfunction (Ibanez and Simi, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Inhibition of p75NTR signaling has emerged as an attractive strategy for limiting neural damage in neurodegeneration and nerve injury.
source: Inhibition of p75NTR signaling has emerged as an attractive strategy for limiting neural damage in neurodegeneration and nerve injury.
evidence: This is a statement about the therapeutic potential based on established knowledge.

claim: The mechanism of activation of p75NTR in response to neurotrophins involves a conformational rearrangement of disulfide-linked receptor dimers, resulting in the separation of intracellular DDs.
source: The mechanism of activation of p75NTR in response to neurotrophins involves a conformational rearrangement of disulfide-linked receptor dimers, resulting in the separation of intracellular DDs (Vilar et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: FRET experiments have shown that the two DDs in the p75NTR dimer are in close proximity to each other (high FRET state).
source: Fluorescence resonance energy transfer (FRET) experiments have shown that the two DDs in the p75NTR dimer are in close proximity to each other (high FRET state) and that NGF binding induces a decrease in FRET signal (Vilar et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: NGF binding to p75NTR induces a decrease in FRET signal between the DDs.
source: Fluorescence resonance energy transfer (FRET) experiments have shown that the two DDs in the p75NTR dimer are in close proximity to each other (high FRET state) and that NGF binding induces a decrease in FRET signal (Vilar et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Disruption of the conformational change through mutation of a conserved cysteine residue in the TM domain prevents p75NTR signaling in response to neurotrophins.
source: Disruption of this conformational change through mutation of a conserved cysteine residue in the TM domain prevents p75NTR signaling in response to neurotrophins (Vilar et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: p75NTR lacks an associated catalytic activity.
source: p75NTR lacks an associated catalytic activity.
evidence: This is established knowledge about p75NTR.

claim: Signaling by p75NTR proceeds via ligand-induced recruitment and release of cytoplasmic effectors to and from its intracellular domain.
source: Similar to other members of the TNFRSF, signaling by p75NTR proceeds via ligand-induced recruitment and release of cytoplasmic effectors to and from its intracellular domain.
evidence: This is established knowledge about p75NTR signaling mechanism.

claim: Three sets of solvent-exposed residues in the p75NTR DD are critical for p75NTR's ability to engage the RhoA, NF-kB and JNK/cell death pathways, respectively.
source: To begin addressing these questions, our laboratory performed a comprehensive structure–function study of the p75NTR DD that resulted in the identification of three sets of solvent-exposed residues that are critical for p75NTR's ability to engage the RhoA, NF-kB and JNK/cell death pathways, respectively (Charalampopoulos et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to previous work from the authors' laboratory.

claim: Receptor mutants that are selectively deficient in one pathway but not others were generated for p75NTR.
source: Receptor mutants that are selectively deficient in one pathway but not others were generated, demonstrating that different signaling outputs can be genetically separated in p75NTR.
evidence: This statement refers to previous work from the authors' laboratory.

claim: Different signaling outputs can be genetically separated in p75NTR.
source: demonstrating that different signaling outputs can be genetically separated in p75NTR.
evidence: This statement is based on previous mutagenesis studies.

claim: RhoGDI interacts constitutively with the DD of unliganded p75NTR.
source: RhoGDI interacts constitutively with the DD of unliganded p75NTR, linking the receptor to the RhoA pathway (Yamashita and Tohyama, 2003).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Neurotrophin binding induces the release of RhoGDI from p75NTR.
source: Neurotrophin binding induces the release of RhoGDI from p75NTR and decreases RhoA activity (Gehler et al., 2004; Yamashita et al., 1999; Yamashita and Tohyama, 2003).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Neurotrophin binding decreases RhoA activity.
source: Neurotrophin binding induces the release of RhoGDI from p75NTR and decreases RhoA activity (Gehler et al., 2004; Yamashita et al., 1999; Yamashita and Tohyama, 2003).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Residues in helices H1 and H6 of the p75NTR DD are critical for its interaction with RhoGDI and RhoA activation.
source: Using biochemical and cell-based assays, we have previously identified solvent-exposed residues in the p75NTR DD that are critical for its interaction with RhoGDI and RhoA activation, including residues in helices H1 and H6 (Charalampopoulos et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to previous work from the authors' laboratory.

claim: The solution structure of the human p75NTR DD:RhoGDI complex was determined by multidimensional nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy.
source: In order to obtain a molecular understanding of this interaction, we determined the solution structure of the human p75NTR DD:RhoGDI complex by multidimensional nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy (Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Table 1).
evidence: The manuscript presents NMR data and structural statistics for the complex.

claim: Human and rat p75NTR DD share more than 90% sequence identity.
source: Human and rat p75NTR DD share more than 90% sequence identity—including all functionally relevant residues—and an essentially identical three-dimensional structure with an overall RMSD of 1.7 Å ((Liepinsh, 1997) and this study).
evidence: This statement is based on sequence comparison and structural data.

claim: Human and rat p75NTR DD have an essentially identical three-dimensional structure with an overall RMSD of 1.7 Å.
source: Human and rat p75NTR DD share more than 90% sequence identity—including all functionally relevant residues—and an essentially identical three-dimensional structure with an overall RMSD of 1.7 Å ((Liepinsh, 1997) and this study).
evidence: This statement is based on structural comparison.

claim: p75NTR DD in the complex with RhoGDI consists of one 310-helix followed by six α-helices.
source: p75NTR DD in the complex consists of one 310-helix followed by six α-helices and its global fold is very similar to that of our previously described structure of rat p75NTR DD (Liepinsh, 1997).
evidence: This is based on the NMR structure determination.

claim: The global fold of p75NTR DD in the complex with RhoGDI is very similar to that of the previously described structure of rat p75NTR DD.
source: p75NTR DD in the complex consists of one 310-helix followed by six α-helices and its global fold is very similar to that of our previously described structure of rat p75NTR DD (Liepinsh, 1997).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison.

claim: In the DD:RhoGDI complex, the C-terminal domain of RhoGDI primarily displays an immunoglobulin-like fold.
source: In the complex, the C-terminal domain of RhoGDI primarily displays an immunoglobulin-like fold similar to previously described structures of this protein (Longenecker et al., 1999).
evidence: This is based on the NMR structure and comparison to previous structures.

claim: Residues Glu40 to Gly57 in the RhoGDI N-terminal domain fold into a long helix in the DD:RhoGDI complex.
source: Residues Glu40 to Gly57 in the RhoGDI N-terminal domain fold into a long helix, which is not involved in p75NTR DD binding and remains flexible in the complex (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is based on the NMR structure.

claim: The N-terminal helix of RhoGDI (residues Glu40 to Gly57) is not involved in p75NTR DD binding.
source: Residues Glu40 to Gly57 in the RhoGDI N-terminal domain fold into a long helix, which is not involved in p75NTR DD binding and remains flexible in the complex (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is based on the NMR structure.

claim: Removal of the N-terminal domain of RhoGDI did not affect RhoGDI binding to p75NTR DD.
source: Removal of this N-terminal domain did not affect RhoGDI binding to p75NTR DD (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on NMR binding experiments.

claim: The interface in the DD:RhoGDI complex is mainly formed by α-helices H1 and H6 of the p75NTR DD and β-strands S2, S3, S9 and α-helix H2 of RhoGDI.
source: Inspection of the interface in the complex showed that it is mainly formed by α-helices H1 and H6 of the p75NTR DD and β-strands S2, S3, S9 and α-helix H2 of RhoGDI, forming a small hydrophobic core surrounded by polar residues (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the NMR structure.

claim: The DD:RhoGDI interface forms a small hydrophobic core surrounded by polar residues.
source: Inspection of the interface in the complex showed that it is mainly formed by α-helices H1 and H6 of the p75NTR DD and β-strands S2, S3, S9 and α-helix H2 of RhoGDI, forming a small hydrophobic core surrounded by polar residues (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the NMR structure.

claim: Charged residues play an important role in the DD:RhoGDI binding interface.
source: Charged residues play an important role in the binding interface and high concentration of salt (i.e., greater than 200 mM NaCl) can almost completely disrupt p75NTR DD:RhoGDI interaction in vitro (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is based on NMR experiments showing salt-dependent disruption of the complex.

claim: High concentration of salt (greater than 200 mM NaCl) can almost completely disrupt p75NTR DD:RhoGDI interaction in vitro.
source: Charged residues play an important role in the binding interface and high concentration of salt (i.e., greater than 200 mM NaCl) can almost completely disrupt p75NTR DD:RhoGDI interaction in vitro (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is based on NMR experiments.

claim: All functional DD determinants previously identified by site-directed mutagenesis clustered at the DD:RhoGDI interface of the complex structure.
source: It is gratifying to note that all functional DD determinants that we have previously identified by site-directed mutagenesis clustered at the DD:RhoGDI interface of the complex structure (labeled red in Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This is based on comparison of the structure with previous mutagenesis data.

claim: Alanine substitution of Asp412, Lys343 or Glu420 in the p75NTR DD significantly diminished interaction with RhoGDI.
source: In the p75NTR DD, substitution of either Asp412, Lys343 or Glu420 was found to significantly diminish interaction with RhoGDI (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is based on co-immunoprecipitation experiments in transfected cells.

claim: Substitution of Lys99 or Lys199 in RhoGDI abolished its interaction with p75NTR.
source: In RhoGDI, substitution of Lys99 or Lys199 abolished its interaction with p75NTR (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is based on co-immunoprecipitation experiments in transfected cells.

claim: Lys99 and Lys199 in RhoGDI make charge interactions with Glu420 and Asp412, respectively, in the p75NTR DD.
source: In agreement with this, the structure of the complex shows that these two positively charged side chains make charge interactions with Glu420 and Asp412, respectively, in the p75NTR DD (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the NMR structure.

claim: p75NTR DD and RhoA interact with different surfaces in RhoGDI, located at opposite sides of the molecule.
source: Analysis of the p75NTR DD:RhoGDI complex and a previously described crystal structure of the RhoGDI:RhoA(GDP) complex (Longenecker et al., 1999) indicated that p75NTR DD and RhoA interact with different surfaces in RhoGDI, located at opposite sides of the molecule.
evidence: This is based on comparison of the NMR structure with a previous crystal structure.

claim: A heterotrimer complex p75NTR DD:RhoGDI:RhoA is structurally feasible.
source: The two distant binding sites on RhoGDI suggested that a heterotrimer complex p75NTR DD:RhoGDI:RhoA may be structurally feasible.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis and HADDOCK modeling.

claim: HADDOCK calculations of the p75NTR DD:RhoGDI:RhoA trimer converged to a mean backbone RMSD of 0.64 ± 0.05 Å.
source: We investigated this by performing HADDOCK calculations (Dominguez et al., 2003) using our solution structure of p75NTR DD from its complex with RhoGDI and the crystal structure of the RhoGDI:RhoA(GDP) complex. Multiple refinements converged to a mean backbone root mean square deviation (RMSD) of 0.64 ± 0.05 Å (Figure 2A,B and Table 2).
evidence: This is based on computational modeling.

claim: The tripartite complex p75NTR DD:RhoGDI:RhoA occupies an energetically preferred conformation according to Ramachandran plot analysis.
source: Ramachandran plot analysis of the docking model indicated that the trimer structure, including the two intermolecular interfaces, still occupies the energetically preferred conformation.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of the HADDOCK model.

claim: In the tripartite complex, the N-terminal domain of RhoGDI folded into two helices and bound to RhoA(GDP), similar to its conformation in the RhoGDI:RhoA(GDP) complex.
source: In the tripartite complex, the N-terminal domain of RhoGDI folded into two helices and bound to RhoA(GDP), similar to its conformation in the RhoGDI:RhoA(GDP) complex (Longenecker et al., 1999).
evidence: This is based on the HADDOCK model and comparison to previous structures.

claim: The DD binding site on RhoGDI remained nearly identical in the tripartite complex compared to the DD:RhoGDI complex.
source: The DD binding site on RhoGDI remained nearly identical to that in the DD:RhoGDI complex.
evidence: This is based on comparison of the HADDOCK model to the NMR structure.

claim: RhoA can be co-immunoprecipitated with p75NTR in the presence of RhoGDI.
source: This analysis shows that interaction of the three proteins can indeed occur simultaneously and explains previous biochemical studies showing that RhoA can be co-immunoprecipitated with p75NTR in the presence of RhoGDI (Yamashita et al., 1999).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to previous literature and is consistent with the structural model.

claim: The binding Kd of RhoGDI to RhoA is 0.14 ± 0.01 μM.
source: Using the purified proteins, we determined the binding affinity of the RhoGDI:RhoA complex by surface plasmon resonance (SPR). Titration of RhoGDI onto immobilized RhoA, yielded a binding Kd of 0.14 ± 0.01 μM, which is in agreement with previous measurements (Tnimov et al., 2012) (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is based on SPR measurements.

claim: When RhoGDI is precomplexed with purified p75NTR DD, the Kd for RhoA binding is 2.2 ± 0.11 μM.
source: Interestingly, when RhoGDI was precomplexed with purified p75NTR DD, the Kd was 2.2 ± 0.11 μM (Figure 2D)
evidence: This is based on SPR measurements.

claim: Binding to the p75NTR DD decreases the affinity of the RhoGDI:RhoA interaction by about 15-fold.
source: indicating that binding to the p75NTR DD decreases the affinity of the RhoGDI:RhoA interaction by about 15-fold.
evidence: This is based on comparison of SPR measurements.

claim: No binding between p75NTR DD and RhoA could be detected in the absence of RhoGDI.
source: We note that, in the absence of RhoGDI, no binding between p75NTR DD and RhoA could be detected in these experiments (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is based on SPR experiments.

claim: RhoGDI binding to the p75NTR DD weakens its interaction with RhoA, which may facilitate RhoA activation.
source: These results suggest that RhoGDI binding to the p75NTR DD weakens its interaction with RhoA, a step which may facilitate RhoA activation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the SPR data.

claim: NGF binding to p75NTR elicits the recruitment of RIP2 kinase to the receptor.
source: NGF binding to p75NTR elicits the recruitment of RIP2 kinase to the receptor.
evidence: This is established knowledge about p75NTR signaling.

claim: Recruitment of RIP2 is required for regulation of the NF-kB pathway by p75NTR.
source: Recruitment of RIP2 is required for regulation of the NF-kB pathway by p75NTR.
evidence: This is established knowledge about p75NTR signaling.

claim: The interaction between p75NTR and RIP2 is mediated by their DD and CARD domains, respectively.
source: Previous biochemical studies established that the interaction between p75NTR and RIP2 is mediated by their DD and CARD domains, respectively (Khursigara et al., 2001).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The RIP2 CARD consists of 107 amino acids and is located in the C-terminal of the protein.
source: The RIP2 CARD consists of 107 amino acids and is located in the C-terminal of the protein.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis.

claim: The RIP2 CARD connects to the N-terminal kinase domain via a linker of 120 amino acids.
source: It connects to the N-terminal kinase domain via a linker of 120 amino acids.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis.

claim: The NMR structure of human RIP2 CARD in monomeric form was determined.
source: We determined the NMR structure of human RIP2 CARD in monomeric form (Figure 3A,B and Table 1).
evidence: The manuscript presents NMR data and structural statistics.

claim: The solution structure of RIP2 CARD comprises an arrangement of six α-helices followed by one short 310-helix.
source: The solution structure of RIP2 CARD comprises an arrangement of six α-helices followed by one short 310-helix, all tightly packed around a hydrophobic core.
evidence: This is based on the NMR structure.

claim: A C-terminal tail of 17 amino acids (Leu524-Met540) follows the RIP2 CARD and is unstructured and flexible in solution.
source: A C-terminal tail of 17 amino acids (Leu524-Met540) follows the CARD and is unstructured and flexible in solution.
evidence: This is based on the NMR structure.

claim: A unique segment (Gln518-Ile523) between the C-terminal tail and the 310-helix in RIP2 CARD contains two structural disruptor residues (Pro519 and Pro520) and lacks a secondary structure.
source: A unique segment (Gln518-Ile523) between the C-terminal tail and the 310-helix contains two structural disruptor residues (i.e., Pro519 and Pro520, Figure 3B) and lacks a secondary structure, but its orientation was well-defined in the NMR structure.
evidence: This is based on the NMR structure.

claim: The most similar structure to RIP2 CARD is the CARD of nucleotide-binding oligomerization domain-containing protein 1 (NOD1), with a Z-score between 9 and 11.
source: Structural comparison using the DALI server (Holm and Rosenström, 2010) showed that the most similar structure to RIP2 CARD was the CARD of nucleotide-binding oligomerization domain-containing protein 1 (NOD1), with a Z-score between 9 and 11.
evidence: This is based on computational structural comparison.

claim: NOD1 and RIP2 interact with each other through their CARDs to propagate immune signaling.
source: NOD1 and RIP2 have been shown to interact with each other through their CARDs to propagate immune signaling (Mayle et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: RIP2 CARD and NOD1 CARD share similar structural features, including a similar arrangement of all but the last of the α-helices.
source: The two CARDs share similar structural features, including a similar arrangement of all but the last of the α-helices, which displays different local secondary structures in the two proteins (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison.

claim: RIP2 CARD has many more charged residues on its surface than NOD1 CARD.
source: Despite their folding similarities, the two CARDs exhibit significantly different surface characteristics. Particularly, RIP2 CARD has many more charged residues on its surface than its NOD1 counterpart (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis.

claim: Different electrostatic surfaces confer different interaction specificities among members of the DD superfamily, including the CARD subfamily.
source: Different electrostatic surfaces will confer different interaction specificities, a common feature among members of the DD superfamily, including the CARD subfamily.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on structural analysis and general knowledge.

claim: The NMR structure of the p75NTR DD:RIP2 CARD complex was determined.
source: In order to obtain a molecular understanding of the p75NTR DD:RIP2 CARD interaction, we determined the NMR structure of the complex.
evidence: The manuscript presents NMR data and structural statistics.

claim: The core helical structure of the p75NTR DD in the DD:CARD complex is similar to that in the DD:RhoGDI complex, with a pairwise RMSD of ~1.9 Å.
source: The core helical structure of the p75NTR DD in the p75NTR DD:RIP2 CARD complex was similar to that in the p75NTR DD:RhoGDI complex, with a pairwise RMSD of ~1.9 Å (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison.

claim: The orientation of α-helices H3 and H6 in p75NTR DD changed by approximately 7°–8° between the DD:RhoGDI and DD:CARD complexes.
source: The orientation of α-helices H3 and H6 changed by approximately 7°–8°.
evidence: This is based on structural comparison.

claim: Pairwise RMSD between RIP2 CARD in monomeric form and in complex with the p75NTR DD is ~1.5 Å.
source: Similarly, pairwise RMSD between RIP2 CARD in monomeric form and in complex with the p75NTR DD was ~1.5 Å (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison.

claim: The main interface in the core structure of the p75NTR DD:RIP2 CARD complex involves α-helices H2, H3, H5, H6, and H5–H6 loop of p75NTR DD and α-helices H1, H3–H4, and H5–H6 loops of RIP2 CARD.
source: The main interface in the core structure of the p75NTR DD:RIP2 CARD complex involved α-helices H2, H3, H5, H6, and H5–H6 loop of p75NTR DD and α-helices H1, H3–H4, and H5–H6 loops of RIP2 CARD (Figure 3E,F).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the NMR structure.

claim: Both electrostatic and hydrophobic interactions contribute to the p75NTR DD:RIP2 CARD interface.
source: Both electrostatic and hydrophobic interactions contribute to the p75NTR DD:RIP2 CARD interface.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the NMR structure.

claim: The C-terminal tail of RIP2 CARD is better defined in its complex with the p75NTR DD compared to its monomeric form.
source: Interestingly, the C-terminal tail of RIP2 CARD was better defined in its complex with the p75NTR DD compared to its monomeric form, although the last six amino acids still remained flexible.
evidence: This is based on comparison of NMR structures.

claim: The C-terminal tail of RIP2 CARD binds to α-helices H1, H5, and H6 of p75NTR DD through both hydrophobic and charged interactions.
source: The C-terminal tail bound to α-helices H1, H5, and H6 of p75NTR DD, through both hydrophobic and charged interactions (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the NMR structure.

claim: Residues Asp357, His361, Glu365 in helix H2, Gln369 and Glu371 in helix H3, Asp399 in helix H5, and Asp412 and Glu415 in helix H6 of p75NTR DD are critical for its interaction with RIP2.
source: In our previous site-directed mutagenesis studies of the p75NTR DD, we had identified residues in helices H2 (Asp357, His361, and Glu365), H3 (Gln369 and Glu371), H5 (Asp399), and H6 (Asp412 and Glu415) as being critical for its interaction with RIP2 (Charalampopoulos et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to previous work from the authors' laboratory.

claim: All residues previously identified as critical for RIP2 interaction mapped to the DD:CARD binding interface in the NMR structure.
source: We were pleased to note that all these residues mapped to the DD:CARD binding interface defined in our NMR structure of the complex (labeled red in Figure 3E,F).
evidence: This is based on comparison of the structure with previous mutagenesis data.

claim: Individual substitution of interface residues Gln437, Asp467, Lys471, Ile496, Glu500, or Arg528 in RIP2 CARD significantly diminished RIP2 interaction with p75NTR.
source: We found that individual substitution of interface residues Gln437, Asp467, Lys471, Ile496, Glu500, or Arg528, significantly diminished RIP2 interaction with p75NTR (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is based on co-immunoprecipitation experiments in transfected cells.

claim: The DD interfaces used for binding to RhoGDI and RIP2 CARD share partially overlapping binding sites on p75NTR DD.
source: Comparison of the DD interfaces used for binding to RhoGDI and RIP2 CARD showed that these shared partially overlapping binding sites on p75NTR DD (Figure 4A)
evidence: This is based on structural comparison.

claim: RIP2 and RhoGDI cannot bind to the p75NTR DD simultaneously due to steric hindrance.
source: indicating that RIP2 and RhoGDI cannot bind to the p75NTR DD simultaneously due to steric hindrance.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis showing overlapping binding sites.

claim: The Kd of RhoGDI binding to the p75NTR DD is 0.82 ± 0.3 μM.
source: The Kd of RhoGDI binding to the p75NTR DD was 0.82 ± 0.3 μM
evidence: This is based on SPR measurements.

claim: The Kd of RIP2 CARD binding to the p75NTR DD is 4.67 ± 0.7 nM.
source: while the Kd of CARD binding to the DD was 4.67 ± 0.7 nM (Figure 4B,C)
evidence: This is based on SPR measurements.

claim: RIP2 CARD binds with approximately 177-fold higher affinity than RhoGDI to the p75NTR DD.
source: indicating that RIP2 CARD binds with approximately 177-fold higher affinity than RhoGDI to the p75NTR DD.
evidence: This is based on comparison of SPR measurements.

claim: The buried solvent accessible area in the p75NTR DD:RIP2 CARD complex is approximately 1400 Å2.
source: This is in line with the larger buried solvent accessible area in the p75NTR DD:RIP2 CARD complex (~1400 Å2) compared to that in the p75NTR DD:RhoGDI complex (~900 Å2).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis.

claim: The buried solvent accessible area in the p75NTR DD:RhoGDI complex is approximately 900 Å2.
source: This is in line with the larger buried solvent accessible area in the p75NTR DD:RIP2 CARD complex (~1400 Å2) compared to that in the p75NTR DD:RhoGDI complex (~900 Å2).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis.

claim: RIP2 CARD associates with the p75NTR DD with faster on-rate and dissociates with slower off-rate than RhoGDI.
source: Kinetic analyses revealed that CARD associates with the p75NTR DD with faster on-rate, and dissociates with slower off-rate, than RhoGDI (Table 3).
evidence: This is based on SPR kinetic analysis.

claim: RIP2 CARD without the C-terminal tail can still fold into a typical α-helical structure.
source: The RIP2 CARD could still fold into a typical α-helical structure after deletion of the C-terminal tail (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is based on CD spectroscopy.

claim: The binding affinity of RIP2 CARD without the C-terminal tail to the p75NTR DD is 58.7 ± 8.8 nM, approximately 12-fold lower than with the C-terminal tail.
source: However, the binding affinity of this construct to the p75NTR DD was 58.7 ± 8.8 nM, that is, approximately 12-fold lower than with the C-terminal tail (Figure 3—figure supplement 4B)
evidence: This is based on SPR measurements.

claim: The C-terminal tail of RIP2 CARD makes a significant contribution to the association of RIP2 with p75NTR.
source: indicating a significant contribution of the C-terminal tail to the association of RIP2 with p75NTR.
evidence: This is based on comparison of binding affinities with and without the C-terminal tail.

claim: RIP2 CARD can displace RhoGDI from the p75NTR DD as demonstrated by 2D NMR competition studies.
source: The differential binding of RhoGDI and RIP2 CARD to the p75NTR DD was further tested through analysis of 2D NMR spectra of RhoGDI binding to p75NTR DD in competition with RIP2 CARD. Figure 4D shows details of the RhoGDI spectra focusing on representative residues located in and/or close to the DD:RhoGDI interface. Addition of p75NTR DD produced a shift in the cross-peaks of these residues (red in Figure 4D), indicating binding of RhoGDI to the DD. Addition of RIP2 CARD to the RhoGDI:DD complex shifted these cross-peaks back to their initial positions (arrows in Figure 4D), indicating dissociation of RhoGDI from the p75NTR DD. These data demonstrate that RhoGDI and RIP2 CARD compete for binding to the p75NTR DD and that RIP2 CARD can displace RhoGDI from the receptor.
evidence: This is based on NMR competition experiments.

claim: Coexpression of RIP2 decreased RhoA-GTP levels in a concentration-dependent manner in cells transfected with p75NTR.
source: In order to test the functional significance of the antagonism between RIP2 and RhoGDI, we assessed the levels of RhoA-GTP, a measure of RhoA activation, in cells transfected with a p75NTR expression construct in the absence or presence of increasing concentrations of a RIP2 construct (Figure 4E). While expression of p75NTR increased RhoA-GTP levels in transfected cells, coexpression of RIP2 decreased RhoA-GTP levels in a concentration-dependent manner (Figure 4E)
evidence: This is based on RhoA activation assays in transfected cells.

claim: RIP2 has an inhibitory role in p75NTR-mediated activation of the RhoA pathway.
source: in agreement with an inhibitory role of RIP2 in p75NTR-mediated activation of the RhoA pathway.
evidence: This is based on functional assays showing RIP2 decreases RhoA activation.

claim: Elevated levels of RhoA-GTP were found in brain extracts from Rip2 knockout mice compared to wild type littermates.
source: In line with this, we found elevated levels of RhoA-GTP in brain extracts from Rip2 knockout mice compared to wild type littermates (Figure 4F)
evidence: This is based on RhoA activation assays in mouse brain extracts.

claim: RIP2 can restrict the activation of the RhoA pathway in vivo.
source: suggesting that RIP2 can also restrict the activation of the RhoA pathway in vivo.
evidence: This is based on data from Rip2 knockout mice.

claim: Purified rat p75NTR DD exists in either monomeric form or equilibrium between monomeric and dimeric forms depending on pH and counterion.
source: Purified rat p75NTR DD has been shown to exist in either monomeric form or equilibrium between monomeric and dimeric forms depending on pH and counterion (Vilar et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Human p75NTR DD exists mainly in monomeric form in TRIS or HEPES buffer at pH 6.0–7.0.
source: We also found that human p75NTR DD exists mainly in monomeric form in TRIS or HEPES buffer at pH 6.0–7.0, which were the buffer conditions used for structure determination of DD:RhoGDI and DD:CARD complexes.
evidence: This is based on NMR observations.

claim: In phosphate buffer, a new form of p75NTR DD was observed corresponding to a dimer.
source: In phosphate buffer, however, we observed a new form of p75NTR DD as revealed by the appearance of a new set of cross peaks in the [1H-15N] HSQC spectrum (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B). The set of cross peaks corresponding to monomeric DD was still visible, with nearly identical chemical shift but weaker intensity (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), suggesting the coexistence of dimeric and monomeric DDs under these conditions.
evidence: This is based on NMR observations.

claim: Dynamic light scattering (DLS) indicated the formation of dimeric p75NTR DDs in the presence of phosphate ions.
source: Dynamic lighter scattering (DLS) also indicated the formation of dimeric p75NTR DDs in the presence of phosphate ions (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: This is based on DLS measurements.

claim: The apparent Kd of p75NTR DD dimerization derived from anisotropic change is 49 ± 15 µM.
source: EGFP-tagged p75NTR DDs showed anisotropic changes due to homodimerization at different DD concentrations. The apparent Kd of dimerization derived from anisotropic change was 49 ± 15 µM (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is based on FRET anisotropy measurements.

claim: The relatively low-affinity interaction of the p75NTR DD homodimer may facilitate DD separation (low FRET state) upon receptor activation by neurotrophins.
source: This relatively low-affinity interaction may facilitate DD separation (low FRET state) upon receptor activation by neurotrophins.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the measured binding affinity.

claim: The NMR structure of the p75NTR DD homodimer was determined.
source: In order to identify the dimerization interface, we determined the NMR structure of the p75NTR DD homodimer.
evidence: The manuscript presents NMR data and structural statistics.

claim: The p75NTR DD homodimer adopts C2 symmetry.
source: The p75NTR DD homodimer adopted a C2 symmetry (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This is based on the NMR structure.

claim: A short C-terminal tail of 7 amino acids (Ser421-Val427) in each monomer of the DD homodimer remains disordered.
source: A short C-terminal tail of 7 amino acids (Ser421-Val427) in each monomer remained disordered, similar to the DD:RhoGDI and DD:CARD complexes.
evidence: This is based on the NMR structure.

claim: The helical bundle of p75NTR DD did not undergo significant structural change in the homodimer with an RMSD lower than 1.5 Å compared to the other complexes.
source: The helical bundle, including the 310 helix, did not undergo significant structural change with an RMSD lower than 1.5 Å compared to the other complexes.
evidence: This is based on structural comparison.

claim: The dimerization interface of the p75NTR DD homodimer consists of α-helices H2 and H3 as well as residues in the H1–H2 and H3–H4 loops.
source: The dimerization interface consisted of α-helices H2 and H3 as well as residues in the H1–H2 and H3–H4 loops.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the NMR structure.

claim: Dimerization of p75NTR DD involves both charge and hydrophobic interactions.
source: Dimerization involved both charge and hydrophobic interactions.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the NMR structure.

claim: The key residues in the p75NTR DD dimer interface include Asp357, Arg360, Thr377, His378, Glu379, and Ala380.
source: The key residues in the dimer interface included Asp357, Arg360, Thr377, His378, Glu379, and Ala380 (corresponding to Asp354, Arg358, Thr375, His376, Glu377, and Ala378 in rat p75NTR DD).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the NMR structure.

claim: The key residues in the human p75NTR DD dimer interface are in agreement with previous site-directed mutagenesis and NMR titration studies of the rat p75NTR DD homodimer.
source: This is in agreement with previous site-directed mutagenesis and NMR titration studies of the rat p75NTR DD homodimer (Vilar et al., 2014) (red-labeled residues in Figure 5C).
evidence: This is based on comparison with previous studies.

claim: Cys381 in the p75NTR DD dimer interface appears in reduced form with a Cβ chemical shift of 26.5 ppm.
source: Cys381 (homologous to Cys379 in rat p75NTR DD) was also located in the dimerization interface but appeared in reduced form with a Cβ chemical shift of 26.5 ppm.
evidence: This is based on NMR chemical shift analysis.

claim: The distance between Cys381Sγ from each monomer in the p75NTR DD homodimer is 6.7 ± 0.1 Å, too long for the formation of a disulfide bond.
source: The distance between Cys381Sγ from each monomer was 6.7 ± 0.1 Å, that is, too long for the formation of a disulfide bond.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the NMR structure.

claim: The two p75NTR DD protomers form a low-affinity, noncovalent homodimer.
source: We conclude that the two p75NTR DD protomers form a low-affinity, noncovalent homodimer in our structure.
evidence: This is based on the NMR structure and biophysical characterization.

claim: The buried solvent accessible area in the p75NTR DD homodimer is 573 Å2.
source: The buried solvent accessible area in the p75NTR DD homodimer was 573 Å2, in line with the low affinity of the DD:DD interaction.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis.

claim: The p75NTR DD homodimer interface does not overlap with the RhoGDI binding site.
source: The p75NTR DD homodimer interface defined in our NMR studies did not overlap with the RhoGDI binding site (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison.

claim: The constitutive interaction of RhoGDI with the closed conformation of p75NTR is consistent with the non-overlapping DD homodimer and RhoGDI binding interfaces.
source: This is in agreement with the constitutive interaction of RhoGDI with the closed conformation of the receptor.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on structural analysis.

claim: The p75NTR DD homodimer partially occludes the RIP2 CARD interaction surface.
source: On the other hand, the DD homodimer partially occluded the RIP2 CARD interaction surface (Figure 6C)
evidence: This is based on structural comparison.

claim: Interaction of RIP2 with p75NTR requires dissociation of the DD homodimer.
source: indicating that interaction of RIP2 with p75NTR requires dissociation of the DD homodimer.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis showing overlap between dimer interface and CARD binding site.

claim: Application of NGF to cells expressing wild type p75NTR produced large oscillations of increased anisotropy at the cell membrane.
source: Application of NGF to cells expressing wild type p75NTR produced large oscillations of increased anisotropy at the cell membrane (Figure 6D), resulting in a positive net change averaged over a 15-min treatment compared to vehicle (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is based on real-time homo-FRET anisotropy measurements.

claim: NGF treatment of cells expressing wild type p75NTR results in a positive net change in anisotropy averaged over 15 minutes compared to vehicle.
source: Application of NGF to cells expressing wild type p75NTR produced large oscillations of increased anisotropy at the cell membrane (Figure 6D), resulting in a positive net change averaged over a 15-min treatment compared to vehicle (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is based on real-time homo-FRET anisotropy measurements.

claim: Increased anisotropy indicates ligand-triggered separation of receptor intracellular domains.
source: As anisotropy is inversely related to FRET, this behavior indicates ligand-triggered separation of receptor intracellular domains, as proposed earlier (Vilar et al., 2009).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the anisotropy data based on the relationship between anisotropy and FRET.

claim: The p75NTR construct carrying mutations in the CARD binding site (CBS mutant) produced very similar anisotropy changes after NGF treatment as wild type p75NTR.
source: Importantly, the p75NTR construct carrying mutations in the CARD binding site (CBS mutant) produced very similar anisotropy changes after NGF treatment (Figure 6D,E)
evidence: This is based on real-time homo-FRET anisotropy measurements.

claim: Recruitment of RIP2 is not required for DD separation in response to ligand binding to p75NTR.
source: indicating that recruitment of RIP2 is not required for DD separation in response to ligand binding to p75NTR.
evidence: This is based on comparison of anisotropy changes in wild type and CBS mutant p75NTR.

claim: The DD homodimer interface overlaps with several residues involved in neurotrophin-mediated activation of JNK, caspase-3 and the apoptosis pathway.
source: Finally, we note that the DD homodimer interface also overlapped with several residues involved in neurotrophin-mediated activation of JNK, caspase-3 and the apoptosis pathway (Figure 6F) as identified in our previous studies (Charalampopoulos et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison with previous mutagenesis data.

claim: Dissociation of the p75NTR DD homodimer is required for recruitment of RIP2 in response to neurotrophins.
source: Thus, while the structure and biochemical properties of the p75NTR DD homodimer support the ligand-independent interaction of RhoGDI with the receptor, they also demonstrate that dissociation of the p75NTR DD homodimer is required for recruitment of RIP2 and for activation of the JNK/caspase-3 pathway in response to neurotrophins.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis showing overlap between dimer interface and CARD binding site.

claim: Dissociation of the p75NTR DD homodimer is required for activation of the JNK/caspase-3 pathway in response to neurotrophins.
source: Thus, while the structure and biochemical properties of the p75NTR DD homodimer support the ligand-independent interaction of RhoGDI with the receptor, they also demonstrate that dissociation of the p75NTR DD homodimer is required for recruitment of RIP2 and for activation of the JNK/caspase-3 pathway in response to neurotrophins.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis showing overlap between dimer interface and JNK/caspase-3 activation sites.

claim: None of the binding surfaces in the p75NTR DD (or in RIP2 CARD) show a close match to any of the six conserved surfaces that characterize classical type I, II, and III interactions in the DD superfamily.
source: Remarkably, none of the binding surfaces in the p75NTR DD (or in RIP2 CARD) identified in this study show a close match to any of the six conserved surfaces that characterize classical type I, II, and III interactions in the DD superfamily.
evidence: This is based on structural comparison with known DD interaction types.

claim: The p75NTR DD surface that binds RhoGDI is formed by residues in helices H1 and H6.
source: The p75NTR DD surface that binds RhoGDI is formed by residues in helices H1 and H6.
evidence: This is based on the NMR structure of the DD:RhoGDI complex.

claim: A previous study proposing helix 5 as a binding site to RhoGDI based on serial deletion analysis is not supported by the solution structure of the DD:RhoGDI complex.
source: A previous study had proposed helix 5 as a binding site to RhoGDI based on serial deletion analysis of the p75NTR DD (Yamashita and Tohyama, 2003). This conclusion is not supported by our solution structure of the DD:RhoGDI complex, in which H5 appears at the opposite side of the interface (Figure 2B), nor by previous structure–function studies (Charalampopoulos et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on comparison of the NMR structure with previous deletion studies.

claim: The surface in the p75NTR DD that interacts with the CARD of RIP2 includes residues in helices H2, H3, and H6 plus residues in the H5–H6 loop.
source: The surface in the p75NTR DD that interacts with the CARD of RIP2 includes residues in helices H2, H3, and H6 plus residues in the H5–H6 loop.
evidence: This is based on the NMR structure of the DD:CARD complex.

claim: Residues in helix H1 as well as the H3–H4 and H5–H6 loops form the binding surface on the CARD of RIP2 for interaction with p75NTR DD.
source: On the other side of this interaction, residues in helix H1 as well as the H3–H4 and H5–H6 loops form the binding surface on the CARD of RIP2.
evidence: This is based on the NMR structure of the DD:CARD complex.

claim: The p75NTR DD:RIP2 CARD complex represents the first structural characterization of an heterotypic interaction in the DD superfamily.
source: To the best of our knowledge, this p75NTR DD:RIP2 CARD complex represents the first structural characterization of an heterotypic interaction in the DD superfamily.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the finding based on knowledge of the field.

claim: An additional interaction between residues in the C-terminal half of helix H5 of the p75NTR DD and the C-terminal tail of RIP2 confers approximately fivefold increased binding affinity.
source: Our solution structure of this complex also revealed an additional interaction between residues in the C-terminal half of helix H5 of the p75NTR DD and the C-terminal tail of RIP2, which extends beyond the RIP2 CARD. This additional contact confers approximately fivefold increased binding affinity between the two proteins.
evidence: This is based on the NMR structure and SPR measurements comparing binding with and without the C-terminal tail.

claim: The interface that mediates the p75NTR DD homodimer involves residues located in helix H3 as well as the H1–H2 and H3–H4 loops.
source: Finally, the interface that mediates the p75NTR DD homodimer involves residues located in helix H3 as well as the H1–H2 and H3–H4 loops.
evidence: This is based on the NMR structure of the DD homodimer.

claim: The p75NTR DD homodimer interface is similar, but not identical, to the type IIIb surface identified in the DD of PIDD for interaction with RAIDD.
source: This surface is similar, but not identical, to the type IIIb surface, like the one identified in the DD of PIDD for interaction with RAIDD (Park et al., 2007b).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison.

claim: Unlike the classical type IIIb surface, the DD:DD interaction in p75NTR makes extensive use of residues in the H3 helix.
source: Unlike the classical type IIIb surface, however, the DD:DD interaction in p75NTR makes extensive use of residues in the H3 helix
evidence: This is based on structural analysis.

claim: The same surface in the two interacting DDs is used to form a symmetric dimer in p75NTR.
source: and the same surface in the two interacting DDs is used to form a symmetric dimer.
evidence: This is based on the NMR structure of the DD homodimer.

claim: The solution structure of the p75NTR DD homodimer shows it is a symmetric, noncovalent dimer held together by low-affinity interactions.
source: The solution structure of the p75NTR DD homodimer shows it is a symmetric, noncovalent dimer held together by low-affinity interactions involving residues in helix H3 and the H1–H2 and H3–H4 loops.
evidence: This is based on the NMR structure and biophysical characterization.

claim: The p75NTR DD dimer structure is in accordance with a recent mutagenesis study that identified residues important for dimerization of rat p75NTR DD.
source: This p75NTR DD dimer structure is also in accordance with a recent mutagenesis study that identified residues important for dimerization of rat p75NTR DD (Vilar et al., 2014), many of which are also implicated in our structure.
evidence: This is based on comparison with previous mutagenesis studies.

claim: The results do not support two crystallographic structures reported for the rat p75NTR DD homodimer that suggested it to be either a covalent symmetric dimer or a noncovalent asymmetric dimer.
source: On the other hand, our results do not support two crystallographic structures reported for the rat p75NTR DD homodimer that suggested this to be either a covalent symmetric dimer, held by a disulfide bond between Cys379 residues, or a noncovalent asymmetric dimer (Qu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is based on comparison of the NMR structure with previous crystal structures.

claim: None of the currently available evidence derived from structural, mutagenesis, or functional studies appears to support the crystal structures reported by Qu et al., 2013.
source: None of the currently available evidence derived from structural, mutagenesis, or functional studies appears to support those crystal structures.
evidence: This is a statement about the weight of evidence against previous structures.

claim: A recent study has suggested that p75NTR can form trimers in transfected cells based on the apparent molecular weights of p75NTR species in SDS/PAGE.
source: A recent study has suggested that p75NTR can form trimers in transfected cells based on the apparent molecular weights of p75NTR species in SDS/PAGE (Anastasia et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: NMR studies of the p75NTR DD do not support the conclusion that p75NTR forms trimers.
source: Our NMR studies of the p75NTR DD do not support such conclusion as we have not found any evidence for the existence of DD trimers in any of the conditions tested.
evidence: This is based on NMR observations.

claim: A recent study used solution NMR spectroscopy to investigate the mobility of the transmembrane and intracellular domains of p75NTR incorporated into lipid–protein nanodisks.
source: Another recent study has used solution NMR spectroscopy to investigate the mobility of the transmembrane and intracellular domains of p75NTR incorporated into lipid–protein nanodisks (Mineev et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: A high level of flexibility in the juxtamembrane domain of p75NTR was found in a recent NMR study.
source: These authors found a high level of flexibility in the juxtamembrane domain of p75NTR, an observation that we also reported in our earlier NMR studies of this domain (Liepinsh, 1997)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Mineev et al. could not detect self-association of intracellular domains of p75NTR in lipid–protein nanodisks.
source: but they could not detect self-association of intracellular domains.
evidence: This statement refers to findings from a previous study.

claim: It is unclear whether the lipid detergent used to form lipid–protein nanodisks interacted with the p75NTR DD and prevented its dimerization.
source: However, it is unclear whether the lipid detergent used to form the lipid–protein nanodisks interacted with the p75NTR DD and prevented its dimerization.
evidence: This is speculation about potential experimental artifacts in a previous study.

claim: The structural studies show that the p75NTR DD and RhoA bind on opposite sides of the RhoGDI molecule, allowing the formation of a tripartite DD:RhoGDI:RhoA complex.
source: Our structural studies show that the p75NTR DD and RhoA bind on opposites sides of the RhoGDI molecule, allowing the formation of a tripartite DD:RhoGDI:RhoA complex.
evidence: This is based on the NMR structure and HADDOCK modeling.

claim: Association of RhoGDI with the p75NTR DD reduced its affinity for RhoA by 15-fold.
source: Our SPR experiments showed that association of RhoGDI with the p75NTR DD reduced its affinity for RhoA by 15-fold.
evidence: This is based on SPR measurements.

claim: Close comparison of RhoGDI structures in the complexes with either p75NTR DD or RhoA revealed local structural perturbations in RhoGDI.
source: Close comparison of RhoGDI structures in the complexes with either p75NTR DD or RhoA revealed local structural perturbations in RhoGDI (Figure 2—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is based on structural comparison.

claim: There is a potential allosteric mechanism underlying the release and activation of RhoA upon RhoGDI binding to p75NTR.
source: suggesting a potential allosteric mechanism underlying the release and activation of RhoA upon RhoGDI biding to the receptor.
evidence: This is speculation based on structural observations.

claim: At the plasma membrane, p75NTR forms a dimer held together by interactions between its DD and TM domains.
source: At the plasma membrane, the p75NTR forms a dimer held together by interactions between its DD and TM domains (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is part of a model based on the structural and functional data presented.

claim: Recruitment of the RhoGDI:RhoA complex brings RhoA close to the plasma membrane.
source: Recruitment of the RhoGDI:RhoA complex brings RhoA close to the plasma membrane (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is part of a model based on the structural data.

claim: RhoGDI binding to the p75NTR DD weakens its interaction with RhoA, allowing RhoA to equilibrate with the plasma membrane where it can be activated by membrane-associated GEFs.
source: RhoGDI binding to the p75NTR DD weakens its interaction with RhoA, a lipid-modified protein, allowing it to equilibrate with the plasma membrane where it can be activated by membrane-associated guanine nucleotide exchange factors (GEFs) (Garcia-Mata et al., 2011).
evidence: This is part of a model based on the structural and biochemical data.

claim: RhoA may be in equilibrium between the cell membrane and the RhoGDI:p75NTR complex.
source: RhoA may thus be in equilibrium between the cell membrane and the RhoGDI:p75NTR complex
evidence: This is part of a model based on the structural and biochemical data.

claim: The action of GEFs and GAPs may contribute to the dynamics of RhoA exchange between membrane and RhoGDI:p75NTR complex.
source: and the action of GEFs and GTPase-activating proteins (GAPs) may further contribute to the dynamics of this exchange (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is speculation about additional factors that may influence the proposed mechanism.

claim: Upon dissociation from p75NTR, RhoGDI regains high affinity for RhoA, extracting it from the membrane and holding it back in the cytosol in an inactive state.
source: Upon dissociation from p75NTR, for example, as a consequence of RIP2 recruitment in response to NGF binding, RhoGDI regains high affinity for RhoA, extracting it from the membrane and holding it back in the cytosol in an inactive state (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is part of a model based on the structural and biochemical data.

claim: This new view of the p75NTR DD in the activation of RhoA is in better agreement with the emerging role of RhoGDI as a general facilitator of small GTPase activity cycles.
source: This new view of the p75NTR DD in the activation of RhoA is in better agreement with the emerging role of RhoGDI as a general facilitator of small GTPase activity cycles.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in the context of current understanding of RhoGDI function.

claim: Recruitment of RIP2 to p75NTR ultimately leads to increased NF-kB activity by as yet unknown mechanisms.
source: Recruitment of RIP2 to p75NTR ultimately leads to increased NF-kB activity by as yet unknown mechanisms.
evidence: This is a statement about current knowledge gaps.

claim: TRAF6 is a known regulator of the NF-kB pathway.
source: Another p75NTR interactor, TRAF6, is also a known regulator of the NF-kB pathway (Khursigara et al., 1999; Ye et al., 1999).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: TRAF6 interacts with the juxtamembrane region of p75NTR, but not with the DD.
source: As TRAF6 has been shown to interact with the juxtamembrane region of p75NTR, but not with the DD
